archives-brief.text: Welcome back. Two parcels arrived on this machine as zip files, and one of them is locked with a password. Let's open both.

archives-extract.text: Now unpack it. Type unzip, then the file name. If it asks whether to replace files, answer Y for yes.

archives-extract-done.text: A new supplies folder appeared, and the zip file is still there too.

archives-finale.text: Lesson two complete. You're ready for the tests. Start with test one, then take on the vault.

archives-find.text: First, go to your Downloads folder and see what arrived.

archives-find-done.text: Two zip files. A zip archive packs lots of files into one, like a parcel.

archives-locked.text: Go back to Downloads and unzip the locked parcel. When it asks for the password, type it and press Enter. You won't see it as you type. That's normal on Linux.

archives-locked-done.text: Unlocked. A wrong password would simply change nothing, so you can always try again.

archives-manifest.text: The parcel came with a manifest. Read it.

archives-manifest-done.text: The second parcel is locked, and the password is on a hidden sticky note on your Desktop.

archives-note.text: The locked parcel unpacked a new folder. Read what is inside.

archives-note-done.text: Both parcels delivered. You can now open any zip file, even a locked one.

archives-peek.text: Before opening a parcel, check what's inside. Type unzip, space, dash L, then the file name. Dash L means list.

archives-peek-done.text: Now you know what is inside, and nothing has been unpacked yet.

archives-sticky.text: Go to your Desktop and find the hidden sticky note. Remember, hidden files need L S dash A.

archives-sticky-done.text: The password is lantern. Remember it.

ciphers-brief.text: Welcome to the cipher room. There is a coded message, a download to check, and a locked file. Along the way you will learn the difference between encoding, hashing and encryption.

ciphers-decode.text: Type base 64, dash D for decode, then message dot B 6 4.

ciphers-decode-done.text: The passphrase is moonlight. Remember: encoding is not secret. Anyone can decode it.

ciphers-decrypt.text: Go back home. Vault dot T X T dot G P G is encrypted. Type G P G, dash D for decrypt, then the file name. When it asks, type the passphrase you decoded. It stays hidden as you type.

ciphers-decrypt-done.text: Decrypted. Unlike Base 64, this was impossible without the passphrase. That is the difference between encoding and encryption.

ciphers-encode.text: Now encode something yourself. Echo the word hello and pipe it into base 64.

ciphers-encode-done.text: That is hello in Base 64. Every computer in the world would encode it exactly the same way.

ciphers-encrypt.text: Now lock your own diary. Type G P G, dash C, then diary dot T X T. Choose a passphrase, and type it twice.

ciphers-encrypt-done.text: Your diary is locked in diary dot T X T dot G P G. But careful: the original, unlocked file is still there.

ciphers-finale.text: Lesson six complete. Encoding is for moving data, hashing is for checking it, and encryption is for keeping it secret. You are ready for the final exam.

ciphers-hash.text: Go to downloads. Before running anything you downloaded, check it. Type S H A 2 5 6 sum, then installer dot S H. It prints a fingerprint called a hash.

ciphers-hash-done.text: That long code is the file's fingerprint. Change a single letter in the file, and it changes completely.

ciphers-look.text: There is a message here. Read message dot B 6 4.

ciphers-look-done.text: It looks like gibberish, but it is Base 64. A way of writing any data with plain letters and numbers.

ciphers-shred.text: Encryption is pointless if the original is still lying around. Delete the plain diary dot T X T.

ciphers-shred-done.text: Only the encrypted copy is left. Your secrets are safe.

ciphers-verify.text: Now check it against the official fingerprint. Type S H A 2 5 6 sum, dash C for check, then installer dot S H A 2 5 6.

ciphers-verify-done.text: O K. The file is exactly what its author published. If anyone had tampered with it, this would say failed.

exploring-brief.text: Welcome, rookie. You've just entered an unfamiliar Linux machine, and the terminal is your only tool. Let's explore it together.

exploring-cat.text: Let's read the note. Type cat, then the file name: notes dot T X T. Cat prints what's inside a file.

exploring-cat-done.text: That is what the note says. Press Escape whenever you want to close it.

exploring-cat-message.text: There's a message in here. Read it.

exploring-cat-message-done.text: You found it. You just explored a Linux machine using nothing but the keyboard. Well done.

exploring-cd.text: Let's go inside Documents. Type C D, then a space, then Documents. C D means change directory.

exploring-cd-done.text: You're inside Documents now. Look at the prompt: it shows where you are.

exploring-cd-hidden.text: You found a hidden folder. Go inside it. You already know how.

exploring-cd-hidden-done.text: Hidden folders work like any other. The dot is just part of the name.

exploring-cd-up.text: Time to go back. Type C D, a space, and two dots. Two dots always mean one level up.

exploring-cd-up-done.text: You're back home. Keep climbing with C D dot dot and you'd reach the root, a single slash: the top of the whole machine.

exploring-finale.text: Lesson one complete. Next, lesson two teaches you how to open zip files, even locked ones.

exploring-ls.text: Now, what's around you? Type L S, short for list, to see what's in this place.

exploring-ls-a.text: Something here is hidden. Type L S, space, dash A. The A means all, so hidden things show up too.

exploring-ls-a-done.text: There it is: dot hidden. Names that start with a dot are hidden from a normal listing. They're not locked, just out of sight.

exploring-ls-docs.text: You're somewhere new. What's in here? Use the command you already know.

exploring-ls-docs-done.text: A text file and another folder. L S always lists the place you are standing in.

exploring-ls-done.text: Three folders appeared. In Linux, folders are called directories.

exploring-pwd.text: First question: where are you? Type P W D. It stands for print working directory, and it tells you exactly where you are.

exploring-pwd-done.text: That's your location. Every command you type runs from here.

files-brief.text: Welcome to your new machine. The last owner left a mess behind. Let's make some space of your own, then clean up.

files-cat-todo.text: Make sure it worked. Read the file.

files-cat-todo-done.text: Perfect. Your words are in the file.

files-cd-proj.text: Now go inside it. You already know how.

files-cd-proj-done.text: You're in. It's empty, for now.

files-echo.text: Echo prints text. The greater than sign sends that text into a file instead of the screen. Type echo, then buy milk in quotes, then greater than, then todo dot T X T.

files-echo-done.text: Your note is saved. One greater than sign replaces a file. Two of them add to the end.

files-finale.text: Lesson three complete. You can create and delete files and folders. Next, you will learn to copy, move and rename them.

files-mkdir.text: Let's make a folder of your own. Type M K D I R, short for make directory, then the name: projects.

files-mkdir-done.text: There it is. A brand new, empty folder called projects.

files-rm.text: Time to clean up. Go back home and remove the junk file. Type R M, short for remove, then junk dot T M P. Careful: Linux has no trash bin. Deleted means gone.

files-rm-done.text: Gone for good. Always double check before you remove something.

files-rm-r.text: Old stuff still has files inside, so rmdir would refuse. Type R M, space, dash R, then old underscore stuff. Dash R means everything inside, too. This is the most powerful delete there is, so use it with care.

files-rm-r-done.text: Everything is cleaned up. Your machine is tidy, and it's yours.

files-rmdir.text: The empty box can go too. Type R M D I R, remove directory, then empty underscore box. It only works on empty folders, which makes it a safe choice.

files-rmdir-done.text: Done. Rmdir refuses to delete a folder with things inside, so it can never surprise you.

files-touch.text: Time for a file. Type touch, then todo dot T X T. Touch creates an empty file.

files-touch-done.text: Your file exists. It's empty, so let's put something in it.

files-whoami.text: First, who does this machine think you are? Type who am I, all as one word.

files-whoami-done.text: You're logged in as rookie. Everything in your home folder belongs to you.

mole-brief.text: Final exam, analyst. Someone inside headquarters is leaking secrets at night. The logs, a coded message, and a locked staff list hold the answer. Find the mole, and file your report.

mole-success.text: Report filed. Felix Morrow, badge B 77. Case closed, analyst. You have completed every mission.

organize-brief.text: Your Desktop is a mess of photos and documents. Time to organise it, and keep a backup while you are at it.

organize-cp.text: Always keep a backup of important work. Type C P, short for copy, then report dot T X T, then report underscore backup dot T X T.

organize-cp-done.text: Now you have the original and a copy.

organize-cp-r.text: To copy a whole folder, add dash R, just like when you deleted one. Type C P, dash R, photos, then photos underscore backup.

organize-cp-r-done.text: The whole folder was copied, photos and all. Your desk is organised and backed up.

organize-finale.text: Lesson four complete. You can copy, move and rename files, even many at once. Next, you will learn to read and search through files like a detective.

organize-glob.text: Moving photos one at a time is slow. The star is a wildcard: it matches any name. So star dot J P G means every J P G file here. Type M V, star dot J P G, photos slash.

organize-glob-done.text: Every photo, moved with one command. Wildcards save a lot of typing.

organize-look.text: First, go to your Desktop and see what is there.

organize-look-done.text: Photos and documents, all mixed together. Let us sort them.

organize-ls-l.text: Want more detail? Type L S, space, dash L. The L means long: one file per line, with its size and the time it changed.

organize-ls-l-done.text: Now you can see how big each file is, and when it last changed.

organize-mkdir-photos.text: Make a folder called photos, right here on the Desktop.

organize-mkdir-photos-done.text: Now the photos have somewhere to go.

organize-mv.text: Let us move a photo. Type M V, short for move, then beach dot J P G, then photos slash.

organize-mv-done.text: Moved. It flew right into the photos folder.

organize-rename.text: Linux has no rename command. Moving a file to a new name, in the same place, renames it. Type M V, report underscore draft dot T X T, then report dot T X T.

search-brief.text: The website went down in the middle of the night, and it is your job to find out why. The answer is somewhere in the logs.

search-finale.text: Lesson five complete. You can read, count and search through files like a detective. Next, the cipher room: secret codes and encryption.

search-find.text: Settings files often end in dot conf. Find searches folders for files by name. Type find, then the tilde for home, then dash name, then star dot conf in quotes.

search-find-done.text: Found it, deep inside server slash settings. Find saves you from opening folder after folder.

search-grep.text: Grep is a search tool. It shows only the lines that contain your text. Type grep, ERROR in capitals, then app dot log.

search-grep-done.text: Three errors, all about a full disk. One of them says: see backup settings. That is a clue.

search-head.text: Logs can be huge. Head shows just the first ten lines. Type head, then app dot log.

search-head-done.text: Everything looks normal at the start. Trouble usually shows up at the end.

search-history.text: Finally, type history. It lists every command you have typed, in order. Great for remembering how you solved something.

search-history-done.text: Your whole investigation, step by step. Detective work, done.

search-logs.text: Go to the logs folder and see what is there.

search-logs-done.text: App dot log is the website log. It is long, so reading all of it would take a while.

search-pipe.text: Commands can work together. The vertical bar is called a pipe: it sends one command's output into the next. Grep dash I ignores capital letters. Type grep dash I disk app dot log, then a pipe, then W C dash L.

search-pipe-done.text: Five lines. Grep found them and W C counted them. Pipes are one of the most powerful ideas in Linux.

search-read-conf.text: Read the backup settings file. You know where it is now.

search-read-conf-done.text: Backups every five minutes, kept forever. That filled the disk. Case closed.

search-tail.text: The newest lines are at the bottom. Tail shows the end of a file. Type tail, dash N, five, then app dot log.

search-tail-done.text: Errors at the very end. Something filled up the disk.

search-wc.text: How long is this log? Type W C, short for word count, dash L for lines, then app dot log.

search-wc-done.text: Forty two lines. Too many to read one by one. Let us search instead.

unfamiliar-brief.text: This is your first test. A brand new machine, and no instructions. Somewhere inside is a hidden message. Find it.

unfamiliar-success.text: Message found. You did it without a guide. Nicely done.

vault-brief.text: Agent, this is the ultimate test. A locked vault. Its password was split into three parts, and each part is hidden in a file you will not see with a normal listing. Follow the clues, find all three parts, and open the vault. Good luck.

vault-part1.text: Part one found. Two to go.

vault-part3.text: Part three found. You have the whole password. Now open the vault.

vault-success.text: Vault open. Clearance granted. Go inside top secret and read everything.
